scenes.heading: Atoms seek lower energy
scenes.visual_text: Bonding can make a more stable arrangement
scenes.narration: Atoms form bonds when the combined arrangement has lower energy than the separated atoms. For many nonmetals, sharing electrons lets each nucleus attract the same electrons and creates a stable covalent bond.

scenes.heading: Valence electrons matter
scenes.narration: The electrons in an atom's outer shell are called valence electrons. These are the electrons most available for bonding. Filled outer shells are especially stable, so atoms often bond to approach that arrangement.

scenes.heading: A shared pair
scenes.narration: Consider two hydrogen atoms. Each contributes one electron to a shared pair. Both nuclei attract that pair, so each hydrogen effectively gains access to two electrons, filling its first shell.

scenes.heading: More pairs, stronger links
scenes.visual_text:
Single: 1 pair
Double: 2 pairs
Triple: 3 pairs
scenes.narration: Atoms can share one, two, or three electron pairs, producing single, double, or triple bonds. The best arrangement depends on the atoms and geometry, not simply on completing an octet rule.

scenes.heading: The key idea
scenes.visual_text:
Shared electrons attract both nuclei
The molecule reaches lower energy
scenes.narration: Covalent bonding is therefore not atoms consciously seeking shells. It is an electrostatic, lower-energy arrangement in which shared electrons hold nuclei together. The shell model is a useful prediction tool, while energy explains why bonding occurs.
